significance.justification: A verified-true result would license the specific conclusion that drug and medical foundation-model interaction signals obey the claimed contrast—"replacing the substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme" abolishes the signal while a "same-enzyme structural swap" preserves it—and that a shared-enzyme direction causally affects predictions. This combines a form-(iii) conditional invariance/asymmetry relating independently measurable enzyme identity and model signal with a form-(ii) steering claim; it establishes both a behavioral phenomenon and a mechanism and fixes expectations for structurally atypical pairs, same-enzyme controls, and pharmacodynamic interactions rather than merely showing CYP information is decodable. The branches are determinate: failure of the bypass contrast and enzyme-selective steering would rule out robust use of the shared-CYP mechanism and undermine mechanism-based generalization, while success would support it; FDA's Clinical Drug Interaction Studies guidance (2020) confirms that CYP substrate, inhibition, and induction relationships are actual decision variables rather than arbitrary labels. In the topic-substitution check, the generic question of whether scientific mechanisms are represented would not earn this score; the enzyme-swap double dissociation and its cross-pair predictions are the claim-specific increment over the obvious representation-probe hypothesis.

reach.justification: The claim names several reusable handles: the "Shared-Enzyme-Beyond-Structure Index," "Bypass-vs-Same-Enzyme Causal Asymmetry," a "mechanism-based failure predictor," and a recovered "shared-enzyme" steering direction. The counterfactual metrics can be used ex ante to audit or gate a model before relying on it for atypical DDI cases, while steering is chiefly a calibrated intervention; the stated consequence that screening "must be gated by explicit metabolic-pathway checks" is also a concrete deployment rule. After re-extraction on another model, the substantive prediction survives calibration as a relation—different-enzyme bypasses should cause a larger signal drop than structurally matched same-enzyme swaps—although the direction and numerical thresholds themselves need re-estimation; the hypothesis covers drug/medical foundation models and multiple representation modalities rather than one checkpoint. FDA's 2020 guidance identifies drug developers and clinical-pharmacology reviewers who already act on CYP evidence, supporting uptake beyond this interpretability research line; the topic-substitution check does not preserve the score because the transferable bypass audit, advance deployment gate, and predicted asymmetry disappear when the claim-specific mechanism is removed.
